citations.quote:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves and the relations $\le$, $\ll$, $I^{\pm}$, $J^{\pm}$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. All curves below are curves in
that sense.

**(a) Chronology and causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **chronological** when there is
no $p\in M$ with $p\ll p$, equivalently when there is no nonconstant future
timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$. It is **causal**
when there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with
$\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$; a nonconstant future causal curve with equal endpoints
is called a **closed causal curve**, and a closed future timelike curve is
called a **closed timelike curve**.

**(b) Strong causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **strongly causal** when for every
$p\in M$ and every open set $U\subseteq M$ with $p\in U$ there is an open set
$V$ with $p\in V\subseteq U$ such that for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and all $a\le s<t\le b$ with $\gamma(s)\in V$ and
$\gamma(t)\in V$ one has $\gamma([s,t])\subseteq V$. Thus no causal curve can
leave $V$ and later re-enter it; a set $V$ with this property for all causal
curves is called **causally convex for causal curves that meet it twice**.

**(c) Global hyperbolicity.** $(M,g,N)$ is **globally hyperbolic** when it is
strongly causal and for all $p,q\in M$ the **causal diamond**
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact in the subspace topology
([[def-compact-space]]).

**(d) Time functions.** A **time function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a function
$u:M\to\mathbb R$ which is continuous from the manifold topology to the usual topology of
$\mathbb R$: for every $p\in M$ and every open neighborhood $W$ of $u(p)$
there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $p$ with $u(V)\subseteq W$
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). It also satisfies
$u(\gamma(a))<u(\gamma(b))$ for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ that is not constant on $[a,b]$.

**(e) Temporal functions.** A **temporal function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
function $u:M\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]])
whose gradient is past-directed timelike: writing $du$ for its differential
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]) and $\nabla u$ for the vector field
with $g(\nabla u,X)=du(X)$ for every smooth vector field $X$, constructed from
the inverse metric of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], one
has
$$g(\nabla u,\nabla u)<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad du(N)=g(\nabla u,N)>0 .$$
The first inequality says that the gradient is nowhere zero and timelike; the
second fixes it as past-directed for the chosen time orientation. No level set
of a temporal function is asserted here to be a hypersurface or to be
spacelike, and no relation between temporal functions and compactness is
asserted; those claims are proved separately where they are used.

**(f) Scope and conventions.** These are mathematical conditions on the
Lorentzian model. Different sources define global hyperbolicity by equivalent
but differently phrased conditions; this page fixes the formulation of (c)
and proves the implications it uses. In particular no equivalence between
global hyperbolicity and the existence of a Cauchy hypersurface is asserted
by this definition, and the physical reading of strong causality or global
hyperbolicity as predictability of a classical model is adopted only in the
framework postulates.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold that is globally hyperbolic in
the sense of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause
(c): strongly causal and with compact causal diamonds
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ for all $p,q\in M$. Let $h$ be the auxiliary metric of
[[thm-gr-auxiliary-complete-riemannian-metric]] and let $\le$, $J^\pm$ be the
relations of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** the causal relation is closed: if $p_k\le q_k$ for all $k$ and
$p_k\to p$, $q_k\to q$, then $p\le q$; consequently $J^+(x)$ and $J^-(x)$
are closed for every $x$, and so are $J^+(K)$ and $J^-(K)$ for every compact
$K\subseteq M$;

**(b)** for all compact $K_1,K_2\subseteq M$ the set
$J^+(K_1)\cap J^-(K_2)$ is compact.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
globally hyperbolic time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (c)), let
$L_g$ be the Lebesgue Lorentzian length functional on locally absolutely continuous future causal curves
([[lem-gr-normal-neighborhood-length-monotonicity]], with nonzero future causal velocity almost everywhere), and for $q\in M$ define the
**time separation**
$$\tau_q:M\to[0,\infty),\qquad \tau_q(r):=\sup\{L_g(\alpha):\ \alpha \text{ is a future causal curve from } r \text{ to } q\},$$
the supremum over the empty set being $0$; thus $\tau_q(r)>0$ exactly for
$r\in I^-(q)$ and $\tau_q(r)=0$ for $r\notin J^-(q)$.

**(a)** For every $r\in J^-(q)$ one has $0\le\tau_q(r)<\infty$. If $r\ne q$, the supremum is attained by a future causal curve $\gamma$ from $r$ to $q$ with $L_g(\gamma)=\tau_q(r)$. Every such **nondegenerate maximizer** is, up to increasing reparametrization, a causal geodesic, with image in the compact set $J^+(r)\cap J^-(q)$. For $r=q$, $\tau_q(q)=0$ and the constant zero-velocity geodesic is the **degenerate maximizer** by convention. It has image $\{q\}$ and length zero; it is not asserted to belong to the curve class requiring nonzero causal velocity almost everywhere. This separates the reflexive case without changing the separation function or the nondegenerate maximizing claim.

**(b)** Let $V$ be a strictly convex normal neighbourhood of $q$ (as produced
by [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]]) and let $W\subseteq V$ be open and
causally convex in $M$ (every causal curve in $M$ with both endpoints in $W$
is contained in $W$), with $\overline W$ compact and $q\in W$. Then for every
$r\in W\cap I^-(q)$,
$$\tau_q(r)=\sqrt{-g_q\bigl(\exp_q^{-1}(r),\exp_q^{-1}(r)\bigr)},$$
so $\tau_q$ is smooth on $W\cap I^-(q)$ and extends continuously by
$\tau_q(q)=0$ and $\tau_q(r)=0$ for $r\in W\setminus J^-(q)$.

**(c)** On every compact set $K\subseteq M$ the function $\tau_q$ is upper
semicontinuous in the following strong form: for every sequence $r_n\to r$ in
$K$ one has $\limsup_n\tau_q(r_n)\le\tau_q(r)$. If moreover $r\in I^-(q)$,
then $\tau_q(r_n)\to\tau_q(r)$ for every sequence $r_n\to r$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection; its existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Fix
$c>0$. All intervals $I,J$ below have nonempty interior. For a
smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ write $D_t$ for the covariant derivative along
$\gamma$ of [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]] with respect to
$\nabla$ (equivalently, the pullback of the Levi–Civita connection).

1. **Metric pairing.** For smooth sections $V,W$ of the pullback bundle
   $\gamma^*TM$,
   $$\frac{d}{dt}\,g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),W(t)\bigr)=g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(D_tV(t),W(t)\bigr)+g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(V(t),D_tW(t)\bigr).$$
   In particular, if $D_tV=D_tW=0$ on $I$, then $g(V,W)$ is constant on $I$.

2. **Parallel transport.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise smooth curve
   with $a<b$.
   For every $v\in T_{\gamma(a)}M$ there is exactly one continuous piecewise
   smooth section $V$ of $\gamma^*TM$ with $D_tV=0$ on each smooth piece and
   $V(a)=v$; the parallel-transport map
   $P_\gamma:T_{\gamma(a)}M\to T_{\gamma(b)}M$, $v\mapsto V(b)$, is linear,
   bijective, and satisfies
   $g_{\gamma(b)}(P_\gamma v,P_\gamma w)=g_{\gamma(a)}(v,w)$ for all $v,w$.
   For $a=b$, the unique section is its prescribed fibre vector and
   $P_\gamma$ is the identity; no $D_t$ condition is imposed on a singleton.

3. **Geodesic speed and proper time.** Along a geodesic
   $\gamma:I\to M$ ([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]) the function
   $t\mapsto g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))$ is constant. If $\gamma$
   is nonconstant, its tangent is nowhere zero and its causal character
   (timelike, null or spacelike) is constant; a constant geodesic has zero
   tangent and is assigned none of those causal characters. If $\gamma$ is a
   **future-directed timelike geodesic** and
   $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-\lambda^2$ with $\lambda>0$, then for
   $t_0<t_1$ its proper-time increment over $[t_0,t_1]$ is
   $\lambda(t_1-t_0)/c$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]), so proper time is an
   affine parameter. In this parameter its four-velocity is
   $U=(c/\lambda)\gamma'$ and is parallel: $D_\tau U=0$. Proper time is not
   assigned to a past-directed curve by that definition; reversing the
   parameter gives a future-directed timelike geodesic with the same
   (positive) proper-time magnitude. A nonconstant null geodesic has null
   tangent and admits no proper-time parametrization.

4. **Affine reparametrizations.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a geodesic whose
   tangent is nowhere zero, and let $h:J\to I$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto
   its open image with $h'\neq0$. Then $\gamma\circ h$ is a geodesic if and
   only if $h(s)=as+b$ with constants $a\neq0$, $b$; in that case $a$ is the
   constant $h'$, and every affine parameter of this nonconstant geodesic
   arises in this way from a fixed one. If $\gamma$ is constant, then
   $\gamma\circ h$ is constant and hence geodesic for every such $h$; no
   affine restriction on $h$ follows.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
chronological and causal relations $\ll$, $\le$ and the sets $I^\pm$,
$J^\pm$ of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Future and past sets.** A subset $F\subseteq M$ is a **future set**
when $I^+(F)\subseteq F$, where $I^+(F)=\bigcup_{p\in F}I^+(p)$; it is a
**past set** when $I^-(F)\subseteq F$. A future set is **open** when it is
open in the manifold topology; for an open future set one has
$F=I^+(F)$.

**(b) Achronal boundary.** A set $A\subseteq M$ is an **achronal boundary**
when $A=\partial F$ for a future set $F$; this is equivalent to being the boundary of an open future set. Indeed,
put $H:=I^+(F)$. Chronological openness makes $H$ open, and the future-set
property gives $H\subseteq F$. Arbitrarily short future timelike segments
from each $p\in F$ give $p\in\overline H$, so
$\overline H=\overline F$. If $p\in\operatorname{Int}F$, a sufficiently
short past timelike segment ending at $p$ starts inside $F$, hence
$p\in H$; therefore $H=\operatorname{Int}F$. It follows that
$\partial H=\overline H\setminus H=\overline F\setminus\operatorname{Int}F=\partial F$.
The short segments and openness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] and
[[lem-gr-chronology-openness]].

The derived elementary properties and boundary equivalence use
Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) through the stated causal-calculus, chronology
and push-up suppliers. The future/past-set predicates themselves are the
set definitions above.

**(c) Elementary properties.** The following are immediate from the
openness of $I^\pm$ and the transitivity of $\ll$
([[lem-gr-chronology-openness]] clause (a),
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clauses (d) and (f)):

- if $F$ is a future set then its complement is a past set, and conversely;
- $I^\pm(S)$, $J^\pm(S)$ and $\overline{J^\pm(S)}$ are future (respectively
  past) sets for every $S\subseteq M$;
- if $F$ is a future set then $F$ is open if and only if $I^+(F)=F$, and
  then $\partial F$ is achronal. Indeed, if $p,q\in\partial F$ and
  $p\ll q$, openness of the chronological relation gives a neighborhood
  $V$ of $p$ such that every $p'\in V$ satisfies $p'\ll q$. Since
  $p\in\overline F$, choose $p'\in V\cap F$. The future-set property gives
  $q\in I^+(F)\subseteq F$, contradicting $q\in\partial F$;
- a set $S$ is achronal in the sense of
  [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (b) if and only
  if $\overline S$ is achronal, because $I^\pm$ is open in its arguments.

**(d) Scope.** These are set-theoretic definitions inside the smooth
Lorentzian model; they assert nothing about existence of achronal
boundaries with additional regularity, and they carry no physical
interpretation here.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, with the
relations $\ll$, $\le$ and the sets $I^\pm$, $J^\pm$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] and the future and past sets of
[[def-gr-future-and-past-sets]]. Then:

**(a) Openness.** For every $x\in M$ the chronological future $I^+(x)$ and
the chronological past $I^-(x)$ are open subsets of $M$.

**(b) The chronological relation is open.** The set
$$\{(x,y)\in M\times M:\ x\ll y\}$$
is open in the product topology of $M\times M$.

**(c) Closure of future and past sets.** Let $F\subseteq M$ be a future set,
that is $I^+(F)\subseteq F$. Then every $q\in\overline F$ satisfies
$I^+(q)\subseteq F$. Dually, if $P$ is a past set ($I^-(P)\subseteq P$) and
$q\in\overline P$, then $I^-(q)\subseteq P$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$F\subseteq M$ be an open future set, so that $I^+(F)=F$
([[def-gr-future-and-past-sets]] clause (a)), and let $A:=\partial F$ be its
achronal boundary. Then:

**(a) Achronality.** $A$ is closed and achronal: no two distinct points of
$A$ are chronologically related in either direction. Consequently every
future or past timelike curve meets $A$ in at most one point.

**(b) Local Lipschitz graph.** For every $p\in A$ there are a chart
$(U,x)$ of the kind produced by [[lem-gr-dominating-cone-bounds]] clauses (a)
and (d) around $p$, with $x(p)=0$, domination constant $K$, and minorant
coefficient $c=16$, and numbers
$a,\rho>0$ with $W:=x^{-1}\bigl((-a,a)\times B_\rho(0)\bigr)\subseteq U$, such
that for every $z\in B_\rho(0)$ the coordinate vertical line
$$L_z:=x^{-1}\bigl((-a,a)\times\{z\}\bigr)$$
meets $A\cap W$ in exactly one point, and there is a function
$\varphi:B_\rho(0)\to(-a,a)$ with
$$A\cap W=\bigl\{x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z):z\in B_\rho(0)\bigr\},\qquad |\varphi(z)-\varphi(z')|\le\sqrt c\,|z-z'|\quad (z,z'\in B_\rho(0)).$$
Thus $A$ is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function of the spatial
coordinates of the chart.

**(c) Topological hypersurface.** The maps $z\mapsto x^{-1}(\varphi(z),z)$ of
(b), for all points $p\in A$, form a topological atlas on $A$: $A$ is a
topological $3$-manifold in the subspace topology and its inclusion into $M$
is a topological embedding. No smoothness of $A$ is asserted.

**(d) Null measure.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mu$ be a measure on the Borel sets of $M$
which is locally absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure:
whenever $(V,y)$ is a chart and $E\subseteq V$ has $y(E)$ of four-dimensional
Lebesgue measure zero, then $\mu(E)=0$. Then $\mu(A\cap K)=0$ for every
compact $K\subseteq M$. In particular this holds for every smooth positive
volume density on $M$.

Assume Countable Choice for the smooth tangent-bundle and time-orientation conventions of the Lorentzian suppliers. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$. A **spacelike two-surface** is a nonempty smooth embedded two-manifold $S\subset M$ without boundary whose induced metric $q:=\iota^*g$ is positive definite, where $\iota:S\hookrightarrow M$ is the inclusion. It is **closed** when it is additionally compact. The constructions below apply to any such spacelike two-surface; compactness is not required. Its normal bundle is $\mathcal NS=(TS)^\perp$. Work on a nonempty open set $U\subseteq S$ carrying a smooth ordered pair of future null normal fields $\ell,k$ with $g(\ell,\ell)=g(k,k)=0$ and $g(\ell,k)=-2$; such pairs exist locally by the preceding lemma. No global pair is part of the definition unless one is explicitly supplied.

For tangent fields $X,Y$ on $U$, define the null second fundamental form, expansion and shear by
$$\chi_\ell(X,Y):=g(\nabla_X\ell,Y),\qquad \theta_\ell:=\operatorname{tr}_q\chi_\ell,\qquad \sigma_\ell:=\chi_\ell-\frac{\theta_\ell}{2}q.$$
Here $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection; its derivative of a section along $S$ means the pullback connection, equivalently the derivative of any smooth ambient extension along tangent directions. The preceding lemma establishes extension independence, symmetry of $\chi_\ell$, and positive definiteness of the screen metric. A **normal-frame boost** is the change $\ell\mapsto e^f\ell$, $k\mapsto e^{-f}k$ for a smooth real function $f$ on $U$. It leaves $q$ fixed; $\chi_\ell,\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$ scale by $e^f$.

A **null geodesic hypersurface congruence from $U$** along the chosen initial normal field $\ell$ is a smooth map $F:U\times J\to M$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval containing $0$, such that $F(p,0)=p$ and $\partial_\lambda F(p,0)=\ell_p$ for every $p\in U$, each curve $\gamma_p(\lambda):=F(p,\lambda)$ is future-directed and null, and its tangent $\ell:=\partial_\lambda F$ obeys the affine geodesic equation
$$D_\lambda\ell=0$$
along every curve $\gamma_p$; here $D_\lambda$ is the covariant derivative along a curve from [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. For each $p\in U$, let $J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$ be the connected component containing $0$ of the parameter values for which $d(F_\lambda)_p:T_pU\to T_{F(p,\lambda)}M$ is injective and the pullback form $(X,Y)\mapsto g(d(F_\lambda)_pX,d(F_\lambda)_pY)$ is positive definite on $T_pU$. Require, for every $\lambda\in J$, that its variation directions satisfy
$$g_{F(p,\lambda)}\bigl(\ell(p,\lambda),dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)\bigr)=0\qquad(X\in T_pU).$$
Thus its variation directions are orthogonal to $\ell$. For $\lambda\in J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$, the map $F$ has rank three locally near $(p,\lambda)$: its two section directions are spacelike and orthogonal to the nonzero null vector $\ell$. Its local image is a null hypersurface, with tangent space $\ell^\perp$ and induced radical $\mathbb R\ell$, as in [[lem-gr-fx-null-normal-plane-and-screen]]. The parameter $\lambda$ is affine. On each section in $J_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the **screen** is $\mathscr S=\ell^\perp/\mathbb R\ell$ with metric $\bar q([X],[Y])=g(X,Y)$; it is the positive two-dimensional quotient, identified isometrically with the tangent plane of that section by projection. The induced form on the full null hypersurface has radical $\mathbb R\ell$ and has no inverse. All traces and inverses in this definition are taken on the screen.

All screen bundles associated with this congruence are understood as bundles over the parameter domain $U\times J$: the notation $\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ denotes the branch determined by $(p,\lambda)$, so self-intersections do not identify distinct screen fibers. For each $\lambda\in J$, the screen Jacobi map $A_\lambda:T_pS\to\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ sends $X$ to the screen class of the variation field $J_X(\lambda):=dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)$; it is invertible for $\lambda\in J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$. A **focal instant** is a positive parameter in $J$ where $A_\lambda$ loses rank; the **first focal instant**, if it exists, is the least such parameter after $0$. Along an affine generator the screen derivative is $\mathcal D_\ell[X]:=[D_\ell X]$; it is independent of the representative, by the preceding lemma. On $J_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the derivative $A_\lambda'$ is taken using $\mathcal D_\ell$, and the **optical endomorphism** is $B_\lambda:=A_\lambda'A_\lambda^{-1}$. Its **optical expansion** is $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}B$, and its **optical shear** is $\sigma:=B-\frac12\theta\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr S}$. Since the congruence is normal to a null hypersurface, $B$ is self-adjoint. Its antisymmetric part $\omega:=(B-B^*)/2$, called the twist, therefore vanishes. At $\lambda=0$, $B$ is the endomorphism $q^{-1}\chi_\ell$ and these optical quantities agree with $\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$.

No orientation of $M$, $S$, or the screen is required for these constructions. Indeed, if two orthonormal screen frames are related by a real $2\times2$ matrix $O$ with $O^{\mathsf T}O=I_2$, then the endomorphism matrices obey $\widehat B=O^{-1}BO$ and $\widehat\sigma=O^{-1}\sigma O$. Cyclicity of the matrix trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\widehat B=\operatorname{tr}B$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\widehat\sigma^2)=\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^2)=|\sigma|_{\bar q}^2$; the last equality follows by summing the squared entries of the symmetric shear matrix in an orthonormal frame. This includes $\det O=-1$. The screen inner products and the rank of $A_\lambda$ are likewise invariant under changes of frame, so neither the index-form contractions nor the focal condition uses a signed screen area form. The preceding lemma constructs normal pairs using the supplied time orientation and only a local spacelike complement; changing the complement's sign interchanges the two future null rays. No global ordered pair follows. If an orientation is additionally supplied, the same formulas apply on that oriented subclass.

Assume Countable Choice for the smooth tangent-bundle convention in the
Lorentzian suppliers below. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian
four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and let $\iota:S\hookrightarrow M$ be
a smooth embedded two-manifold without boundary whose induced form
$q:=\iota^*g$ is positive definite. Write
$$\mathcal N_pS:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,X)=0\text{ for every }X\in T_pS\}.$$
Then $\mathcal N S$ is a smooth rank-two Lorentzian vector bundle. Around each
$p\in S$ there are smooth future null normal fields $\ell,k$ with
$$g(\ell,\ell)=g(k,k)=0,\qquad g(\ell,k)=-2.$$
On an overlap where two such ordered pairs select the same future null ray,
they differ by a smooth boost $\ell'=e^f\ell$, $k'=e^{-f}k$; if their ray
labels are exchanged, the same rule holds after interchanging the labels.
No global null normal pair is asserted.

Here a **smooth null hypersurface** $H\subset M$ means a smooth embedded
three-dimensional submanifold without boundary such that, at every $p\in H$,
the restriction $g_p|_{T_pH}$ is positive semidefinite of rank two. Its radical
is the one-dimensional subspace
$$\operatorname{Rad}(g_p|_{T_pH}):=\{v\in T_pH:g_p(v,w)=0\text{ for every }w\in T_pH\}.$$
A **smooth future null normal field** on $H$ is a smooth nowhere-zero section
$\ell$ of this radical line, with $g_p(\ell_p,N_p)<0$. Thus
$$T_pH=\ell_p^\perp,\qquad (T_pH)^\perp=\operatorname{Rad}(g_p|_{T_pH})=\mathbb R\ell_p;$$
in particular, the normal space of a null hypersurface is a null line, not a
Lorentzian two-plane. A **spacelike section** $S$ of $H$ is a smooth embedded
two-manifold $S\subset H$ such that $q:=g|_{TS}$ is positive definite and
$$T_pH=T_pS\oplus\mathbb R\ell_p\qquad(p\in S).$$
The condition says that $S$ is transverse to the null generators.
The **null generator curves** are integral curves $\gamma$ of $\ell$, meaning
$\dot\gamma=\ell\circ\gamma$; when $D_\ell\ell=0$, their parameter is affine.
For fields defined only along $H$ or a surface $S$, covariant derivatives
$\nabla_X\ell$ use the pullback of the metric-selected connection.

For a smooth future null normal field $\ell$ on $H$, the quotient
$$\mathscr S_p:=\ell_p^\perp/\mathbb R\ell_p,\qquad p\in H,$$
is a smooth rank-two bundle with positive metric
$$\bar q_p([X],[Y]):=g_p(X,Y).$$
The normal line is $\mathbb R\ell_p$; the auxiliary null direction used in the
proof below is not a second normal to $H$. If $\ell$ is **affinely geodesic**,
meaning $D_\ell\ell=0$ along its integral curves, the map
$$B_p:\mathscr S_p\to\mathscr S_p,\qquad [X]\mapsto[\nabla_X\ell]$$
is well-defined and self-adjoint with respect to $\bar q$, that is,
$\bar q(Bu,v)=\bar q(u,Bv)$. On a spacelike section $S$ of $H$, the quotient
map $T_pS\to\mathscr S_p$, $X\mapsto[X]$, is an isometry; it is an isomorphism
by transversality, and $\bar q([X],[Y])=q(X,Y)$. For a smooth future null
normal $\ell$ to a spacelike surface $S$, define
$$\chi_\ell(X,Y):=g(\nabla_X\ell,Y)\qquad(X,Y\in T_pS);$$
where $\nabla_X\ell$ is computed with the pullback of the metric-selected
connection to $S$. This is a well-defined symmetric bilinear form. Along an
affine generator, for a screen section $[X]$, the screen derivative
$\mathcal D_\ell[X]:=[D_\ell X]$ is independent of the representative and
preserves the screen metric in the sense that
$$\ell\bigl(\bar q([X],[Y])\bigr)=\bar q(\mathcal D_\ell[X],[Y])+\bar q([X],\mathcal D_\ell[Y]).$$
For a smooth function $f$ on the section, the rescaling
$\ell'=e^f\ell$, $k'=e^{-f}k$ of a normalized null normal pair is a boost; it
obeys
$$\chi_{e^f\ell}=e^f\chi_\ell.$$

Assume Countable Choice for the Lorentzian supplier conventions. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, let $S$ be a smooth spacelike two-surface, and let $F:U\times J\to M$ be a smooth null geodesic hypersurface congruence from an open section $U\subseteq S$, as defined in [[def-gr-fx-null-screen-geometry]]. Write $\ell=\partial_\lambda F$ and fix $p\in U$. Before the first focal instant let $A_\lambda:T_pS\to\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ be the screen Jacobi map, $B=A'A^{-1}$ the optical endomorphism, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}B$ its expansion, and $\sigma=B-\frac12\theta\,\mathrm{id}$ its shear. Let $\operatorname{Ric}$ be the Ricci tensor in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Then, along the generator $\gamma(\lambda)=F(p,\lambda)$ and before the first focal instant,
$$\frac{d\theta}{d\lambda}=-\frac{\theta^2}{2}-|\sigma|_{\bar q}^2-\operatorname{Ric}(\ell,\ell).$$
If $\operatorname{Ric}(\ell,\ell)\ge0$ along the generator and $\theta(0)<0$, then a first focal instant occurs by affine parameter
$$\lambda_*=\frac{2}{|\theta(0)|},$$
provided the smooth congruence and generator are defined through $\lambda_*$. Here a focal instant means that the screen Jacobi map loses rank; the conclusion is local along this generator and asserts no curvature singularity.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, as required by the supplied
causal-curve and push-up results. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold. Let $S$ be a smooth embedded two-manifold without
boundary whose induced metric $q:=g|_{TS}$ is positive definite, and let
$p\in S$. Choose an open neighborhood $U\subseteq S$ of $p$ and a smooth
future null normal field $\ell$ along $U$, so
$g(\ell_q,Y)=0$ for every $q\in U$ and $Y\in T_qS$.
Let $\gamma:[0,L_1]\to M$ be smooth up to its endpoints, with
$$\gamma(0)=p,\qquad \dot\gamma(0)=\ell_p,\qquad g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0,\qquad g(\dot\gamma,N)<0,\qquad D_\lambda\dot\gamma=0.$$
Here $D_\lambda$ is covariant differentiation along the curve. Put
$\chi_\ell(X,Y):=g(\nabla_X\ell,Y)$ as in
[[def-gr-fx-null-screen-geometry]], and set $B_0:T_pS\to T_pS$ by
$q(B_0X,Y)=\chi_\ell(X,Y)$ for all $X,Y\in T_pS$.
The screen along $\gamma$ is
$$\mathscr S_\lambda:=\dot\gamma(\lambda)^\perp/\mathbb R\dot\gamma(\lambda),$$
with its positive metric and screen derivative $\mathcal D_\lambda$ from
[[def-gr-fx-null-screen-geometry]]. Define
$$\mathcal R_\lambda[X]:=[R(X,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma].$$
A **normal screen Jacobi field** is a smooth section $J$ of $\mathscr S$ that
satisfies $\mathcal D_\lambda^2J+\mathcal R_\lambda J=0$ and the initial
conditions $J(0)=[X]$, $\mathcal D_\lambda J(0)=B_0X$ for some
$X\in T_pS$. A **focal instant** $\lambda_0\in(0,L_1]$ is a parameter at
which such a field with $X\ne0$ has $J(\lambda_0)=0$.

Put $I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p)$,
$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p)$, and
$E^+(S):=J^+(S)\setminus I^+(S)$, using the causal-reachability conventions
of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

If $\lambda_0$ is a focal instant, let $\widetilde\gamma:I\to M$ be the
unique maximal affine geodesic extension of $\gamma$, where $I$ is an open
interval containing $[0,L_1]$ and
$\widetilde\gamma|_{[0,L_1]}=\gamma$. There is $\varepsilon>0$ with
$[0,\lambda_0+\varepsilon]\subset I$ such that
$$\widetilde\gamma(\lambda)\in I^+(S)\qquad (\lambda_0<\lambda<\lambda_0+\varepsilon).$$
Consequently, no point on this portion of the generator belongs to
$E^+(S)$. The conclusion is local along the generator and does not assert
geodesic incompleteness or curvature blow-up. In an SI interpretation take
$x^0=ct$ and $\lambda$ in metres; the proof itself is independent of units.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ induced by the chart $\psi_p$ on $T_pM$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
geodesics, their maximal domains $I_{q,v}$ and the exponential maps
$\exp_q$ be those of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Fix
$p\in M$. Write $\pi:TM\to M$ for the bundle projection.

**(a) Smoothness of the joint map.** The set
$$\mathcal D:=\{(q,v)\in TM:\ 1\in I_{q,v}\}\subseteq TM$$
is open in $TM$, and the **joint exponential map**
$$\Phi:\mathcal D\longrightarrow M\times M,\qquad \Phi(q,v):=(q,\exp_q v),$$
is smooth.

**(b) Differential at $(p,0)$.** The differential $d\Phi_{(p,0)}$ is an
isomorphism. Explicitly, fix a smooth chart $(U,x)$ around $p$; it induces
the chart $(TU,Tx)$ of $TM$ and the product chart $(U\times U,x\times x)$ of
$M\times M$, and under the induced identifications
$T_{(p,0)}(TM)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ and
$T_{(p,p)}(M\times M)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ one has
$$d\Phi_{(p,0)}(u,w)=(u,\ u+w)\qquad\text{for all }u,w\in T_pM .$$

**(c) Diffeomorphism and two-point inverse.** There are open neighborhoods
$V\subseteq\mathcal D$ of $(p,0)$ and $W\subseteq M\times M$ of $(p,p)$ such
that $\Phi|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Moreover $V$ can be chosen
product-like: there are a chart $(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$, a radius
$r>0$ and a velocity radius $\rho>0$ such that, writing $B_s:=\{y\in\mathbb
R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<s\}$,
$$V=\bigl\{(q,v):\ q\in x^{-1}(B_r),\ \text{the coordinate components of }v\text{ in }(TU,Tx)\text{ lie in }B_\rho\bigr\},$$
and there is $s\in(0,r)$ with $x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\times x^{-1}(\overline{B_s})\subseteq W$.
Consequently the velocity map
$$v:W\longrightarrow TM,\qquad (q,r)\longmapsto v(q,r):=\text{the vector with }(q,v(q,r))\in V,\ \Phi(q,v(q,r))=(q,r),$$
is well defined and smooth, and $\exp_q\bigl(v(q,r)\bigr)=r$ for all
$(q,r)\in W$.

**(d) Lipschitz bound for the two-point inverse.** On every pair
$x^{-1}(B_s)\times x^{-1}(B_s)\subseteq W$ as in (c) there is a constant
$\Lambda\ge 0$ such that, for all $q,r\in x^{-1}(B_s)$,
$$|v(q,r)|_x\le\Lambda\,\bigl|x(q)-x(r)\bigr|_{\mathrm e},$$
where $|v|_x$ denotes the Euclidean norm of the coordinate components of
$v$ and $v(q,q)=0$. In particular $|v(q,r)|_x\le 2\Lambda s$ on this pair.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) and geodesics as in
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $p\in M$ and let
$O\subseteq M$ be an open neighborhood of $p$. Then there are a chart
$(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$ and a radius $r>0$ such that
$C:=x^{-1}(B_r)$, $B_r=\{y\in\mathbb R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<r\}$ based at
$0=x(p)$, is contained in $O$ and has the following properties.

**(a) Normal neighborhood of each point.** For every $q\in C$ define
$$W_q:=\bigl\{u\in\mathcal E_q:\ \exp_q(tu)\in C\ \text{for every }t\in[0,1]\bigr\},$$
where $\mathcal E_q$ is the exponential domain of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (d). Then $W_q$ is an
open star-shaped neighborhood of $0$ in $T_qM$, and
$\exp_q|_{W_q}:W_q\to C$ is a diffeomorphism onto $C$.

**(b) Unique contained joining segment.** For all $q,q'\in C$ there is
exactly one geodesic segment joining $q$ to $q'$ whose image is contained in
$C$, namely
$$x_{q,q'}:[0,1]\to C,\qquad x_{q,q'}(t)=\exp_q\bigl(t\,v(q,q')\bigr),$$
where $v(q,q')$ is the two-point inverse velocity of
[[lem-gr-joint-exponential-diffeomorphism]] clause (c). For $q\ne q'$ the
points $x_{q,q'}(t)$, $0<t<1$, lie in $C$ strictly inside the coordinate
ball, i.e. $|x(x_{q,q'}(t))|_{\mathrm e}<r$; and $x_{q',q}$ is the time
reverse of $x_{q,q'}$ up to affine reparametrization.

**(c) Strict convexity.** In the terminology of
[[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (b), $C$ is a
strictly convex normal neighborhood; in particular the position vector
$P(q,q')=d(\exp_q)_{v(q,q')}\bigl(v(q,q')\bigr)$ and the squared
displacement $D^2(q,q')=g_q\bigl(v(q,q'),v(q,q')\bigr)$ are defined for all
$q,q'\in C$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]). Let $C\subseteq M$ be a strictly
convex normal set ([[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]]
clause (b)), let $p\in C$, and write
$$W_p:=\exp_p^{-1}(C)\subseteq T_pM,\qquad v(q):=\exp_p^{-1}(q),\qquad P(p,q):=d(\exp_p)_{v(q)}(v(q)),\qquad D_p^2(q):=g_p(v(q),v(q)).$$
Define
$$J_C^+(p):=\{p\}\cup\{q\in C:\text{there is a future causal curve } \sigma:[0,1]\to C\text{ with }\sigma(0)=p,\ \sigma(1)=q\},$$
so the reflexive endpoint $p$ is included even though a constant curve is
not in the curve class. Define
$$I_C^+(p):=\{q\in C:\text{there is a future timelike curve } \sigma:[0,1]\to C\text{ with }\sigma(0)=p,\ \sigma(1)=q\}$$
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]). Put
$$\mathcal C^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future causal or }v=0\},\quad \mathcal T^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future timelike}\},\quad \mathcal N^+:=\{v\in W_p:v\text{ is future null and }v\ne0\}.$$
Then:

**(a) Causal containment.** For every future causal curve
$\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ with $\sigma(0)=p$, the position vector
$v(\sigma(t))$ is future causal or zero for every $t\in[0,1]$.

**(b) Cone characterizations.**
$$J^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal C^+),\qquad I^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal T^+),\qquad J^+_C(p)\setminus\bigl(I^+_C(p)\cup\{p\}\bigr)=\exp_p(\mathcal N^+).$$

**(c) Null rigidity.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$, and let $\hat s\in(0,1]$ satisfy: $v(\sigma(\hat s))$ is
future null nonzero and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for every $t\in(0,\hat s]$. Then
there are $v_0\in\mathcal N^+$ and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous
surjection $\varphi:[0,\hat s]\to[0,1]$ with
$\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for $0\le t\le\hat s$.

**(d) Length maximality.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$. Then
$$L_g(\sigma)\le\sqrt{-D_p^2\bigl(\sigma(1)\bigr)}=\sqrt{-g_p\bigl(v(\sigma(1)),v(\sigma(1))\bigr)} .$$
If moreover $v(\sigma(1))$ is future timelike and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for all
$t\in(0,1]$, then equality holds if and only if there are $v_0$ future
timelike and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous surjection
$\varphi:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for all $t$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]) for the absolutely continuous causal-curve
calculus and the supplied causal results used below.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ and the relations $\ll$, $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** if $p\ll q$ and $q\le r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(b)** if $p\le q$ and $q\ll r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(c)** if $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ is a future causal curve and there are
$a\le s<t\le b$ such that $\gamma|_{[s,t]}$ is a future timelike curve, then
$\gamma(a)\ll\gamma(b)$;

**(d)** consequently
$$I^+\bigl(J^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega),\qquad I^-\bigl(J^-(\Omega)\bigr)=I^-(\Omega)$$
for every $\Omega\subseteq M$, and dually
$J^+\bigl(I^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega)$.

No choice principle beyond the stated assumptions is used.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subspaces as in [[def-subspace-topology-top]] and compactness as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **Closed in compact is compact.** If $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed in $X$, then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$.
2. **Finite unions.** If $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K_0, \dots, K_n$ are compact
   subsets of $X$, then $K_0 \cup \dots \cup K_n$ is a compact subset of $X$. The
   union of the empty list is $\varnothing$, which is a compact subset of every
   space.

Claim 1 needs $X$ to be compact and claim 2 does not; no hypothesis of any kind
is placed on $X$ in claim 2. **No choice principle is used**: claim 1 selects
nothing, taking a least index where a selection would be natural, and claim 2
makes finitely many selections through [[lem-finite-choice]], a theorem of ZF.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with metric-selected connection $\nabla$. A **future-directed affinely parametrized null geodesic** is a smooth nonconstant curve $\gamma:J\to M$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with nonempty interior, such that its tangent $\dot\gamma$ is future-directed and null at every interior parameter and $D_\lambda\dot\gamma=0$. Here “null” means $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0$ and $\dot\gamma\ne0$, and future-directed means $g(\dot\gamma,N)<0$. The geodesic equation and covariant derivative are those of the metric-selected connection.

The **maximal future affine interval** of such a geodesic is the future endpoint interval of its maximal extension as an affinely parametrized geodesic in $M$. It is **future complete** when that interval has no finite upper endpoint, equivalently when its affine parameter tends to $+\infty$. The spacetime is **future null geodesically complete** when every future-directed null geodesic is future complete, and **future null geodesically incomplete** when at least one is not.

An affine change of parameter $\widetilde\lambda=a\lambda+b$ with $a>0$ preserves whether the maximal future interval is unbounded above, so these properties do not depend on the chosen positive affine normalization.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{T}_d$ be
its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]]), so that $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a
topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and is metrizable
([[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only
   if** $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a compact topological space
   ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. For every $A \subseteq X$: $A$ is a compact subset of the metric space
   $(X,d)$ if and only if $A$ is a compact subset of the topological space
   $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$, the two readings of "compact subset" being the metric
   subspace $(A, d_A)$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]) and the topological
   subspace $(A, (\mathcal{T}_d)_A)$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Nothing here is a coincidence and nothing is transported.** The open-cover
condition of [[def-metric-compactness]] quantifies over families of subsets open
in $(X,d)$, and by [[def-metric-topology]] those are exactly the members of
$\mathcal{T}_d$; so the two conditions are not merely equivalent, they are the
same condition written twice. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Put $F:=I^+(S)$. It is open because it is the union of the open sets $I^+(s)$, $s\in S$. If $x\in F$ and $x\ll y$, then some $s\in S$ satisfies $s\ll x$; transitivity gives $s\ll y$, so $y\in F$. Thus $F$ is an open future set.

For each point of $S$, choose a neighborhood with the two smooth null normal branches supplied by [F9]. On each branch rescale by a positive smooth factor so that $g(\ell,N)=-1$; this is possible by [F20] and does not change the sign of the expansion by [F8]. Both normalized expansions are continuous and negative at the chosen point by the trapped-surface hypothesis. Shrink the neighborhood so that both are at most $-c_j$ for some $c_j>0$. Compactness of $S$ gives a finite subcover; the minimum of its finitely many positive constants gives $c>0$ such that every normalized future null normal has initial expansion $\theta_0\le -c$.

By [F1] and [F3], $J^+(S)$ is closed, and $F\subseteq J^+(S)$; hence $\overline F\subseteq J^+(S)$. Therefore $\partial F=\overline F\setminus F\subseteq E^+(S)$. Conversely, take $p\in E^+(S)$ and choose $s\in S$ with $s\le p$. The timelike vector $N_p$ and the local exponential map give future timelike points $p_\epsilon\to p$ by [F12], [F14] and [F20]. If $s=p$ then $s\ll p_\epsilon$; if $s\ne p$ then $s\le p\ll p_\epsilon$ and [F15] gives $s\ll p_\epsilon$. Thus $p_\epsilon\in F$ and, since $p\notin F$, $p\in\partial F$. Hence $E^+(S)=\partial F$.

Set $L:=2/c$. For each normalized null normal at $s\in S$, future completeness [F21], local smooth dependence [F16], and smooth evaluation on the maximal geodesic domain [F12] give a smooth null normal geodesic congruence near that initial datum through $[0,L]$. Applying [F10] with $\theta_0\le-c$ and the null Ricci hypothesis gives a first focal parameter $\lambda_f\le 2/|\theta_0|\le L$. The extension required in [F11] is supplied by future null completeness, so its local variation data also exist slightly beyond $\lambda_f$.
Apply [F7] to the open future set $F$. The equality in step 2.1 shows that $E^+(S)$ is closed and is a topological three-manifold without boundary.

Let $p\in E^+(S)$ and choose $s\in S$ with $s\le p$. If $s=p$, use the zero-length segment at $s$. If $s
e p$, [F4] supplies a maximizing causal geodesic $\gamma$ from $s$ to $p$. Since $p
otin I^+(S)$, $s
ot\ll p$, so the maximizing length is zero; the nonconstant affine geodesic has constant squared speed by [F5], and therefore its future causal tangent is null. Rescale its affine parameter by a positive constant so that $g(\dot\gamma(0),N_s)=-1$, and translate the parameter so that its initial value is $0$.

Every point $r$ on this segment satisfies $s\le r\le p$. If $r\in I^+(S)$, some $s'\in S$ satisfies $s'\ll r\le p$; the push-up rule [F15] then gives $s'\ll p$, contradicting $p\notin I^+(S)$. Thus the entire segment lies in $E^+(S)$.

The initial null tangent $\ell=\dot\gamma(0)$ is normal to $S$. Suppose otherwise. Then some $X\in T_sS$ has $g(\ell,X)\ne0$; since $S$ is spacelike, $g(X,X)>0$. Choose a smooth curve $\eta(u)\subset S$ with $\eta(0)=s$ and $\eta'(0)=X$. The joint exponential map lemma [F13] gives a smooth two-point inverse near $(s,s)$ whose differential in local tangent-bundle coordinates at the diagonal sends basepoint/endpoint variations $(X,\ell)$ to $\ell-X$. Therefore, after identifying nearby tangent spaces by a smooth local frame, $v(u,\delta):=\exp_{\eta(u)}^{-1}(\gamma(\delta))=\delta\ell-uX+o(|u|+\delta)$. Choose a small nonzero $a$ with $a\,g(\ell,X)>0$ and $g(\ell-aX,\ell-aX)=-2a g(\ell,X)+a^2g(X,X)<0$. With $u=a\delta$, $v(a\delta,\delta)/\delta\to\ell-aX$, so for sufficiently small $\delta>0$ the vector is timelike; its future orientation follows by continuity from the future null vector $\ell$ for small $|a|$. By [F14], $\eta(a\delta)\ll\gamma(\delta)$. The remaining segment $\gamma|_{[\delta,\lambda_p]}$ is causal; [F15] gives $\eta(a\delta)\ll p$, contradicting $p\notin I^+(S)$. Hence $\ell\perp T_sS$.

Return to $p\in E^+(S)$ and its normal generator from steps 3.2, 4.1, and 5.1, with endpoint parameter $\lambda_p$. If a focal instant $\lambda_f$ occurred strictly before $\lambda_p$, [F11] would give a point $r=\gamma(\lambda)$ with $\lambda_f<\lambda<\lambda_p$ and $r\in I^+(S)$. Since $r\le p$, [F15] would imply $p\in I^+(S)$, a contradiction. Hence $\lambda_p\le\lambda_f\le L$; for $p\in S$ the parameter is $0$ and the same bound holds.

Choose finitely many relatively compact coordinate patches covering $S$, each contained in a patch with the two smooth normalized null normal fields from step 1.2. Their compact closures $K_j$ exist by choosing smaller Euclidean chart balls and applying Heine–Borel [F19] and the continuous-image theorem [F17]. For each $K_j$ and each branch $\ell_{j,\pm}$, the parameter domain $K_j\times[0,L]$ is compact by [F22], and the map $(s,\lambda)\mapsto\exp_s(\lambda\ell_{j,\pm}(s))$ is continuous on it by [F12], [F16] and future completeness. Its image is compact by [F17]. By [F18], the finite union $C$ of these compact images is compact. Step 6.1 shows that every $p\in E^+(S)$ lies in $C$.
By step 3.1, $E^+(S)$ is closed in $M$. Since step 7.1 places it inside the compact set $C$, it is closed in $C$ and hence compact by [F18]. This proves the claim.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves and the relations $\le$, $\ll$, $I^{\pm}$, $J^{\pm}$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. All curves below are curves in
that sense.

**(a) Chronology and causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **chronological** when there is
no $p\in M$ with $p\ll p$, equivalently when there is no nonconstant future
timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$. It is **causal**
when there is no nonconstant future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with
$\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$; a nonconstant future causal curve with equal endpoints
is called a **closed causal curve**, and a closed future timelike curve is
called a **closed timelike curve**.

**(b) Strong causality.** $(M,g,N)$ is **strongly causal** when for every
$p\in M$ and every open set $U\subseteq M$ with $p\in U$ there is an open set
$V$ with $p\in V\subseteq U$ such that for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and all $a\le s<t\le b$ with $\gamma(s)\in V$ and
$\gamma(t)\in V$ one has $\gamma([s,t])\subseteq V$. Thus no causal curve can
leave $V$ and later re-enter it; a set $V$ with this property for all causal
curves is called **causally convex for causal curves that meet it twice**.

**(c) Global hyperbolicity.** $(M,g,N)$ is **globally hyperbolic** when it is
strongly causal and for all $p,q\in M$ the **causal diamond**
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact in the subspace topology
([[def-compact-space]]).

**(d) Time functions.** A **time function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a function
$u:M\to\mathbb R$ which is continuous from the manifold topology to the usual topology of
$\mathbb R$: for every $p\in M$ and every open neighborhood $W$ of $u(p)$
there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $p$ with $u(V)\subseteq W$
([[def-continuous-map-top]]). It also satisfies
$u(\gamma(a))<u(\gamma(b))$ for every future causal curve
$\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ that is not constant on $[a,b]$.

**(e) Temporal functions.** A **temporal function** on $(M,g,N)$ is a smooth
function $u:M\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]])
whose gradient is past-directed timelike: writing $du$ for its differential
([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]) and $\nabla u$ for the vector field
with $g(\nabla u,X)=du(X)$ for every smooth vector field $X$, constructed from
the inverse metric of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]], one
has
$$g(\nabla u,\nabla u)<0\qquad\text{and}\qquad du(N)=g(\nabla u,N)>0 .$$
The first inequality says that the gradient is nowhere zero and timelike; the
second fixes it as past-directed for the chosen time orientation. No level set
of a temporal function is asserted here to be a hypersurface or to be
spacelike, and no relation between temporal functions and compactness is
asserted; those claims are proved separately where they are used.

**(f) Scope and conventions.** These are mathematical conditions on the
Lorentzian model. Different sources define global hyperbolicity by equivalent
but differently phrased conditions; this page fixes the formulation of (c)
and proves the implications it uses. In particular no equivalence between
global hyperbolicity and the existence of a Cauchy hypersurface is asserted
by this definition, and the physical reading of strong causality or global
hyperbolicity as predictability of a classical model is adopted only in the
framework postulates.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold that is globally hyperbolic in
the sense of [[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause
(c): strongly causal and with compact causal diamonds
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ for all $p,q\in M$. Let $h$ be the auxiliary metric of
[[thm-gr-auxiliary-complete-riemannian-metric]] and let $\le$, $J^\pm$ be the
relations of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** the causal relation is closed: if $p_k\le q_k$ for all $k$ and
$p_k\to p$, $q_k\to q$, then $p\le q$; consequently $J^+(x)$ and $J^-(x)$
are closed for every $x$, and so are $J^+(K)$ and $J^-(K)$ for every compact
$K\subseteq M$;

**(b)** for all compact $K_1,K_2\subseteq M$ the set
$J^+(K_1)\cap J^-(K_2)$ is compact.
