Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Subspace topology: the traces of the open sets, its closed sets and its bases, the continuity of the inclusion, and the characteristic property of a map into a subspace). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.
The Euclidean inclusion of $S^n$ induces its round metric. In spherical coordinates on $S^2$, $g=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$.

Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a nonempty open set with global coordinates
$y=(y^0,y^1)$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]),
let $(q_{AB})$ be a smooth symmetric $2\times2$ matrix of functions on $V$
with

$$\Delta_q(y):=\det\bigl(q_{AB}(y)\bigr)<0\qquad(y\in V),$$

so that $q$ is a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $V$ whose value
at every point is nondegenerate with inertia $(1,1,0)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and let $r:V\to(0,\infty)$ be
a smooth function. Indices $A,B,C,D$ run over $\{0,1\}$ and indices
$i,j,k,l$ over the sphere directions below. Define on $V$:

$$(q^{AB}):=(q_{AB})^{-1},\qquad \Gamma^A{}_{BC}:=\tfrac12\sum_Dq^{AD}\bigl(\partial_Bq_{DC}+\partial_Cq_{BD}-\partial_Dq_{BC}\bigr),$$

$$\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r:=\partial_A\partial_Br-\sum_C\Gamma^C{}_{AB}\,\partial_Cr, \qquad \Delta_qr:=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r, \qquad z:=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\partial_Ar\,\partial_Br .$$

Further define

$$R^A{}_{BCD}:=\partial_C\Gamma^A{}_{DB}-\partial_D\Gamma^A{}_{CB} +\sum_E\bigl(\Gamma^A{}_{CE}\Gamma^E{}_{DB}-\Gamma^A{}_{DE}\Gamma^E{}_{CB}\bigr), \qquad R_{ABCD}:=\sum_Eq_{AE}R^E{}_{BCD},$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}:=\sum_{A,C}q^{AC}R_{ABCD},\qquad S_q:=\sum_{B,D}q^{BD}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}.$$

Let $S^2:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean
sphere with its induced smooth structure and round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]],
[[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]), let
$M:=V\times S^2$ carry the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]),
and let $\pi:M\to V$ and $\iota:M\to S^2$ be the projections. Define the
global symmetric covariant $2$-tensor

$$g:=\pi^*q+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$$

on $M$, where $r$ in this formula is pulled back from $V$. In any product
chart $(y^0,y^1,\xi^2,\xi^3)$, let $\gamma_{ij}$ be the round-metric
components of the angular chart. The components of $g$ are

$$g_{AB}:=q_{AB},\qquad g_{Ai}:=0,\qquad g_{ij}:=r^2\,\gamma_{ij} \qquad(A,B\in\{0,1\},\ i,j\in\{2,3\}),$$

Then:

**(a) The metric.** The global pullback formula defines a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ on $M$; at every point it is nondegenerate
with inertia $(3,1,0)$, so
$(M,g)$ is a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(b) Christoffel symbols.** Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection of
$g$, unique by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]
clause (b) ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), and let
$\Gamma^\mu{}_{\nu\rho}$ be its Christoffel symbols in a product chart. Then
the only nonzero symbols, beyond the displayed lower-index symmetry
$\Gamma^\mu{}_{\nu\rho}=\Gamma^\mu{}_{\rho\nu}$, are

$$\Gamma^A{}_{BC}\ \text{of the first display},\qquad \Gamma^i{}_{Aj}=\frac{\partial_Ar}{r}\,\delta^i{}_j,\qquad \Gamma^A{}_{ij}=-r\,q^{AB}\partial_Br\,\gamma_{ij},\qquad \Gamma^i{}_{jk}\ \text{the round-sphere symbols in the chosen chart},$$

In a spherical-polar chart these are $\Gamma^2{}_{33}=-\sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta$
and $\Gamma^3{}_{23}=\Gamma^3{}_{32}=\cot\vartheta$, with all other
$\Gamma^i{}_{jk}$ vanishing. Pole charts use their own round-metric symbols.

**(c) Ricci tensor.** With $\operatorname{Ric}$ the Ricci tensor of $\nabla$
([[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (c)), in every product
chart

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{AB}=\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}-\frac{2}{r}\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r, \qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{Ai}=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=\bigl(1-z-r\Delta_qr\bigr)\gamma_{ij}.$$

**(d) Scope.** The statements are identities of the displayed component
functions in product charts and use no field equation, no vacuum condition and
no sign or positivity assumption on $s$; nothing is asserted about
completeness, geodesics, extensions or the physical reading of the coordinates.
The hypothesis $\Delta_q<0$ is used for nondegeneracy and inertia of $g$; it is
the only signature input.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Let $S\subset M$ be a nonempty smooth embedded two-manifold, compact without boundary, whose induced metric $q$ is positive definite. At each point its normal plane $(T_pS)^\perp$ is a Lorentzian two-plane with two future null rays. On any open patch carrying a smooth ordered pair of future null normals $\ell,k$ with $g(\ell,k)=-2$, define
$$\chi_\ell(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\ell,Y),\qquad \theta_\ell=\operatorname{tr}_q\chi_\ell,\qquad \chi_k(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xk,Y),\qquad \theta_k=\operatorname{tr}_q\chi_k$$
for tangent vectors $X,Y$ to $S$. These are the null second fundamental forms and their expansions. A **future trapped surface** is such an $S$ for which, on every local patch and for both future null normal rays, the corresponding expansion is strictly negative at every point. Positive rescaling of a null normal multiplies its expansion by the same positive factor, so the sign condition is independent of its affine normalization and of a local interchange of the two rays.

Assume Countable Choice for the smooth tangent-bundle and time-orientation conventions of the Lorentzian suppliers. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$. A **spacelike two-surface** is a nonempty smooth embedded two-manifold $S\subset M$ without boundary whose induced metric $q:=\iota^*g$ is positive definite, where $\iota:S\hookrightarrow M$ is the inclusion. It is **closed** when it is additionally compact. The constructions below apply to any such spacelike two-surface; compactness is not required. Its normal bundle is $\mathcal NS=(TS)^\perp$. Work on a nonempty open set $U\subseteq S$ carrying a smooth ordered pair of future null normal fields $\ell,k$ with $g(\ell,\ell)=g(k,k)=0$ and $g(\ell,k)=-2$; such pairs exist locally by the preceding lemma. No global pair is part of the definition unless one is explicitly supplied.

For tangent fields $X,Y$ on $U$, define the null second fundamental form, expansion and shear by
$$\chi_\ell(X,Y):=g(\nabla_X\ell,Y),\qquad \theta_\ell:=\operatorname{tr}_q\chi_\ell,\qquad \sigma_\ell:=\chi_\ell-\frac{\theta_\ell}{2}q.$$
Here $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection; its derivative of a section along $S$ means the pullback connection, equivalently the derivative of any smooth ambient extension along tangent directions. The preceding lemma establishes extension independence, symmetry of $\chi_\ell$, and positive definiteness of the screen metric. A **normal-frame boost** is the change $\ell\mapsto e^f\ell$, $k\mapsto e^{-f}k$ for a smooth real function $f$ on $U$. It leaves $q$ fixed; $\chi_\ell,\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$ scale by $e^f$.

A **null geodesic hypersurface congruence from $U$** along the chosen initial normal field $\ell$ is a smooth map $F:U\times J\to M$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval containing $0$, such that $F(p,0)=p$ and $\partial_\lambda F(p,0)=\ell_p$ for every $p\in U$, each curve $\gamma_p(\lambda):=F(p,\lambda)$ is future-directed and null, and its tangent $\ell:=\partial_\lambda F$ obeys the affine geodesic equation
$$D_\lambda\ell=0$$
along every curve $\gamma_p$; here $D_\lambda$ is the covariant derivative along a curve from [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. For each $p\in U$, let $J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$ be the connected component containing $0$ of the parameter values for which $d(F_\lambda)_p:T_pU\to T_{F(p,\lambda)}M$ is injective and the pullback form $(X,Y)\mapsto g(d(F_\lambda)_pX,d(F_\lambda)_pY)$ is positive definite on $T_pU$. Require, for every $\lambda\in J$, that its variation directions satisfy
$$g_{F(p,\lambda)}\bigl(\ell(p,\lambda),dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)\bigr)=0\qquad(X\in T_pU).$$
Thus its variation directions are orthogonal to $\ell$. For $\lambda\in J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$, the map $F$ has rank three locally near $(p,\lambda)$: its two section directions are spacelike and orthogonal to the nonzero null vector $\ell$. Its local image is a null hypersurface, with tangent space $\ell^\perp$ and induced radical $\mathbb R\ell$, as in [[lem-gr-fx-null-normal-plane-and-screen]]. The parameter $\lambda$ is affine. On each section in $J_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the **screen** is $\mathscr S=\ell^\perp/\mathbb R\ell$ with metric $\bar q([X],[Y])=g(X,Y)$; it is the positive two-dimensional quotient, identified isometrically with the tangent plane of that section by projection. The induced form on the full null hypersurface has radical $\mathbb R\ell$ and has no inverse. All traces and inverses in this definition are taken on the screen.

All screen bundles associated with this congruence are understood as bundles over the parameter domain $U\times J$: the notation $\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ denotes the branch determined by $(p,\lambda)$, so self-intersections do not identify distinct screen fibers. For each $\lambda\in J$, the screen Jacobi map $A_\lambda:T_pS\to\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ sends $X$ to the screen class of the variation field $J_X(\lambda):=dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)$; it is invertible for $\lambda\in J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$. A **focal instant** is a positive parameter in $J$ where $A_\lambda$ loses rank; the **first focal instant**, if it exists, is the least such parameter after $0$. Along an affine generator the screen derivative is $\mathcal D_\ell[X]:=[D_\ell X]$; it is independent of the representative, by the preceding lemma. On $J_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the derivative $A_\lambda'$ is taken using $\mathcal D_\ell$, and the **optical endomorphism** is $B_\lambda:=A_\lambda'A_\lambda^{-1}$. Its **optical expansion** is $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}B$, and its **optical shear** is $\sigma:=B-\frac12\theta\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr S}$. Since the congruence is normal to a null hypersurface, $B$ is self-adjoint. Its antisymmetric part $\omega:=(B-B^*)/2$, called the twist, therefore vanishes. At $\lambda=0$, $B$ is the endomorphism $q^{-1}\chi_\ell$ and these optical quantities agree with $\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$.

No orientation of $M$, $S$, or the screen is required for these constructions. Indeed, if two orthonormal screen frames are related by a real $2\times2$ matrix $O$ with $O^{\mathsf T}O=I_2$, then the endomorphism matrices obey $\widehat B=O^{-1}BO$ and $\widehat\sigma=O^{-1}\sigma O$. Cyclicity of the matrix trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\widehat B=\operatorname{tr}B$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\widehat\sigma^2)=\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^2)=|\sigma|_{\bar q}^2$; the last equality follows by summing the squared entries of the symmetric shear matrix in an orthonormal frame. This includes $\det O=-1$. The screen inner products and the rank of $A_\lambda$ are likewise invariant under changes of frame, so neither the index-form contractions nor the focal condition uses a signed screen area form. The preceding lemma constructs normal pairs using the supplied time orientation and only a local spacelike complement; changing the complement's sign interchanges the two future null rays. No global ordered pair follows. If an orientation is additionally supplied, the same formulas apply on that oriented subclass.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary with affine connection $\nabla$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ is an **affinely parametrized geodesic** when
$$D_t\gamma'(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$
with one-sided interpretation at an included endpoint. Constant curves are geodesics. Unless another parametrization is explicitly stated, “geodesic” means affinely parametrized geodesic.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and let
$S\subseteq M$.

**(a) Spacelike hypersurfaces.** A subset $\Sigma\subseteq M$ is a **spacelike
embedded hypersurface** when it is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
of $M$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) such that the
restriction of $g_p$ to $T_p\Sigma\times T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for
every $p\in\Sigma$; equivalently, every nonzero vector tangent to $\Sigma$ is
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). A spacelike
embedded hypersurface is automatically a nondegenerate hypersurface, so its
$g$-orthogonal complement in $T_pM$ is one-dimensional and nondegenerate, and
it carries a unique future-directed unit timelike normal; that normal is
constructed where it is used, not here.

**(b) Achronality and acausality.** $S$ is **achronal** when no two distinct
points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\ll q$ or $q\ll p$; $S$ is **acausal** when no two
distinct points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\le q$ or $q\le p$. Every acausal set is
achronal, since $p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$.

**(c) Cauchy sets.** $S$ is a **Cauchy set** when for every inextendible
causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ the parameter set
$$\gamma^{-1}[S]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$$
has exactly one element. Because a strictly increasing continuous surjection
of intervals induces a bijection of parameter sets, this condition is
invariant under reparametrization
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (e)); it is stated in terms of
parameters rather than of the point set $\gamma(I)\cap S$, so that a closed
causal curve counts two visits to the same point as two parameter values. A
**Cauchy hypersurface** is a Cauchy set that is also a spacelike embedded
hypersurface in the sense of clause (a).

**(d) Domains of dependence.** For any $S\subseteq M$ define
$$D^+(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve through }p \text{ meets }S\},$$
and dually $D^-(S):=\{p\in M:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve
through }p\text{ meets }S\}$, where "meets $S$" means that some parameter
value is mapped into $S$, and $D(S):=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S)$ is the **domain of
dependence** of $S$.

**(e) Cauchy horizon.** For a closed set $S\subseteq M$ the **future Cauchy
horizon** is
$$H^+(S):=D^+(S)\setminus I^-(D^+(S)),$$
the set of points of $D^+(S)$ that are not chronologically preceded by any
point of $D^+(S)$; dually $H^-(S):=D^-(S)\setminus I^+(D^-(S))$, and the
**Cauchy horizon** is $H(S):=H^+(S)\cup H^-(S)$.

**(f) Scope.** These are mathematical definitions. Neither existence of
Cauchy sets nor any relation between the objects defined here is asserted.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and suppose there exists a Cauchy set
$S\subseteq M$ ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause
(c)): every inextendible causal curve meets $S$ in exactly one parameter
value. Then:

**(a)** there is no nonconstant future causal curve with equal endpoints
(so $(M,g,N)$ is causal and chronological in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (a));

**(b)** $(M,g,N)$ is strongly causal (clause (b) of that definition);

**(c)** for all $p,q\in M$ the causal diamond
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is globally
hyperbolic in the sense of clause (c) of that definition.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subspaces as in [[def-subspace-topology-top]] and compactness as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **Closed in compact is compact.** If $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed in $X$, then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$.
2. **Finite unions.** If $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K_0, \dots, K_n$ are compact
   subsets of $X$, then $K_0 \cup \dots \cup K_n$ is a compact subset of $X$. The
   union of the empty list is $\varnothing$, which is a compact subset of every
   space.

Claim 1 needs $X$ to be compact and claim 2 does not; no hypothesis of any kind
is placed on $X$ in claim 2. **No choice principle is used**: claim 1 selects
nothing, taking a least index where a selection would be natural, and claim 2
makes finitely many selections through [[lem-finite-choice]], a theorem of ZF.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold that is globally hyperbolic, meaning strongly causal with compact causal diamonds. Let $S\subset M$ be a nonempty compact smooth embedded spacelike two-surface whose two future null expansions are negative everywhere. Assume the direct null Ricci condition $\operatorname{Ric}(\ell,\ell)\ge0$ for every null vector $\ell$ and assume every future-directed affinely parametrized null geodesic in $M$ is future complete. Define
$$I^+(S)=\bigcup_{s\in S}I^+(s),\qquad J^+(S)=\bigcup_{s\in S}J^+(s),\qquad E^+(S)=J^+(S)\setminus I^+(S).$$
Then $E^+(S)=\partial I^+(S)$ is a closed topological three-manifold without boundary and is compact in the subspace topology of $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ that is globally hyperbolic (strongly causal with compact causal diamonds). Let $\Sigma\subset M$ be a connected noncompact smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface, meaning that every inextendible causal curve meets $\Sigma$ exactly once. Let $S\subset M$ be a nonempty compact smooth spacelike two-surface on which both future null expansions are negative for the two local future null normal rays. Assume directly that $\operatorname{Ric}_p(v,v)\ge0$ for every point $p\in M$ and every null vector $v\in T_pM$. Then $(M,g,N)$ is future null geodesically incomplete: at least one maximal future-directed affinely parametrized null geodesic has an affine parameter interval with finite upper endpoint. This conclusion asserts no curvature divergence or singular point belonging to $M$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the causal-curve class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Chart independence.** Local absolute continuity in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (a) is independent of the
chosen chart and of the smooth atlas. Every compact parameter interval
admits a finite subdivision on each of whose pieces a chart representative
is absolutely continuous. For a continuous curve, the relative neighborhood
formulation and the compact chart-interval formulation of that definition
are equivalent.

**(b) Velocity and smooth composition.** At every interior parameter value
$t$ at which one chart representative is differentiable, every chart
representative is differentiable, the velocity $\gamma'(t)$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (b) is well defined and
independent of the chart, and the set of parameter values at which some
chart representative is differentiable has full measure in the domain. For
every smooth map $F$ of an open subset of $M$ into a finite-dimensional
smooth manifold $P$ (in particular $P=\mathbb R$) whose domain contains
the image of $\gamma$, the composite $F\circ\gamma$ is locally absolutely
continuous in charts of $P$ using the same relative neighborhood definition,
and $(F\circ\gamma)'(t)=dF_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))$ at almost
every parameter value $t$.

**(c) Piecewise $C^1$ curves.** Every piecewise $C^1$ curve (with the finite
admissible partition and one-sided endpoint convention of clause (a) of
[[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]) is locally absolutely
continuous; a piecewise $C^1$ curve all of whose tangents are future causal
is a future causal curve, and if in addition its tangents are future
timelike, it is a future timelike curve.

**(d) Concatenation.** If $\gamma_1:[a,b]\to M$ and $\gamma_2:[b,c]\to M$ are
future causal curves (respectively future timelike curves) with
$\gamma_1(b)=\gamma_2(b)$, then the concatenation $\gamma:[a,c]\to M$,
$\gamma(t):=\gamma_1(t)$ for $t\le b$ and $\gamma(t):=\gamma_2(t)$ for
$t\ge b$, is a future causal (respectively future timelike) curve; the same
holds for any finite chain of such curves.

**(e) Reparametrization.** If $\varphi:J\to I$ is a strictly increasing
$C^1$ diffeomorphism of intervals with $\varphi'>0$ and $\gamma:I\to M$ is
locally absolutely continuous, then $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is locally
absolutely continuous and $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is future causal (respectively
future timelike) exactly when $\gamma$ is. Moreover $\gamma$ is
future-inextendible if and only if $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is
future-inextendible, and this equivalence holds for every strictly increasing
continuous surjection $\varphi$ of intervals, not only the $C^1$ ones.

**(f) Relations.** The relation $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is reflexive and transitive, and
$p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$ for all $p,q$; the relations $J^{\pm}$ and
$I^{\pm}$ of that definition are therefore nested, $I^{\pm}(S)\subseteq
J^{\pm}(S)$ for every $S\subseteq M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold. Suppose a smooth three-manifold $S_0$ and a smooth diffeomorphism $\Psi:\mathbb R\times S_0\to M$ are supplied such that each curve $s\mapsto\Psi(s,z)$ is an inextendible future timelike curve and $\Psi(0,z)=z$. Let $\Sigma\subset M$ be a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface, meaning that it is met exactly once by every inextendible causal curve. Then the second-coordinate projection
$$P:=\operatorname{pr}_{S_0}\circ\Psi^{-1}\big|_\Sigma:\Sigma\to S_0$$
is a diffeomorphism. In particular, $\Sigma$ and $S_0$ have the same connectedness and compactness properties.

derivations.claim: The map $\Phi_H(\tau,\omega)=(H^{-1}\sinh(H\tau),H^{-1}\cosh(H\tau)\omega)$ is a smooth bijection from $\mathbb R\times S^3$ onto $M_H$. Its inverse is $\tau=H^{-1}\operatorname{arsinh}(HX_0)$ and $\omega=(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)/\sqrt{H^{-2}+X_0^2}$, so it is a diffeomorphism. Pulling back the ambient metric $-dX_0^2+\sum_{i=1}^4dX_i^2$ gives $g=-d\tau^2+a^2\gamma_{S^3}$ with $a=H^{-1}\cosh(H\tau)>0$; hence $g$ is Lorentzian and $N=\partial_\tau$ is a smooth future timelike orientation. Let $\Sigma_0=\{X_0=0\}$ and identify $z_\omega=(0,H^{-1}\omega)\in\Sigma_0$. Then $\Psi(\tau,z_\omega):=\Phi_H(\tau,\omega)$ is a diffeomorphism $\mathbb R\times\Sigma_0\to M_H$ with $\Psi(0,z)=z$; each orbit is future timelike, and $\tau\to\pm\infty$ along its two ends prevents a limit point in $M_H$, so the orbit is inextendible. The unit sphere $S^3$ is compact by [F8] and connected because any two points are joined by a great-circle arc (with an intermediate point chosen for antipodal pairs).

Let $\gamma(s)=(\tau(s),\omega(s))$ be any future causal curve. At almost every parameter its tangent is nonzero future causal, so $\dot\tau>0$ and $a(\tau)^2|\dot\omega|_{\gamma_{S^3}}^2\le\dot\tau^2$. Since $a(\tau)\ge H^{-1}$ and the round metric on $S^3$ is induced from $\mathbb R^4$, every angular component satisfies $|\dot\omega^j(s)|\le H\dot\tau(s)$ almost everywhere. By [F12], for any compact subinterval $[s_1,s_2]$ and each coordinate $j$,
$$|\omega^j(s_2)-\omega^j(s_1)|\le\int_{s_1}^{s_2}|\dot\omega^j(s)|\,ds\le H\bigl(\tau(s_2)-\tau(s_1)\bigr).$$
The function $\tau$ is strictly increasing, since its derivative is positive almost everywhere on every nondegenerate subinterval. If its future endpoint were a finite $b$, then $\tau(s)\uparrow b$ and the four component estimates make each $\omega^j(s)$ Cauchy as $s$ approaches the endpoint. Completeness of $\mathbb R$ gives a limit $\omega_b\in\mathbb R^4$, and continuity of the Euclidean norm gives $|\omega_b|=1$, so $\omega_b\in S^3$. Hence $\gamma(s)\to(b,\omega_b)$ in $M_H$, contradicting the definition of future-inextendibility; the vertical curve $\tau\mapsto(\tau,\omega_b)$ also exhibits a future timelike continuation. The same estimates at a finite past endpoint give a past limit and contradict past-inextendibility. Thus every inextendible causal curve has $\tau$-range $\mathbb R$. Continuity and strict monotonicity make every slice meet it exactly once. Each slice is smooth and spacelike with metric $a(\tau)^2\gamma_{S^3}$; it is compact and connected by [F1], [F8], hence is a compact connected Cauchy hypersurface.

On $0<\chi<\pi$, write $\omega=(\cos\chi,\sin\chi\,\sigma)$ with $\sigma\in S^2$, so $g=q+r^2\gamma_{S^2}$ for $q=-d\tau^2+a^2d\chi^2$ and $r=a\sin\chi$. Directly from the two-dimensional Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^\tau_{\chi\chi}=aa'$ and $\Gamma^\chi_{\tau\chi}=a'/a$, one gets $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{\tau\tau}=-a''/a$, $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{\chi\chi}=aa''$, $\operatorname{Hess}_{\tau\tau}r=a''\sin\chi$, $\operatorname{Hess}_{\chi\chi}r=-a(1+a'^2)\sin\chi$, $z=\cos^2\chi-a'^2\sin^2\chi$, and $\Delta_qr=-a''\sin\chi-(1+a'^2)\sin\chi/a$.

Let $X(\lambda)$ be an affinely parametrized null geodesic on the hyperboloid. The tangential projection of the ambient flat derivative is torsion-free and compatible with the induced metric: projecting $D_UV$ removes only a normal component, which is orthogonal to every tangent field, while the ambient derivative preserves the metric and torsion. By uniqueness of the metric-selected connection, this projected derivative is the geodesic connection. Hence $X''(\lambda)$ is normal to the hyperboloid and is a scalar multiple $f(\lambda)X(\lambda)$. Differentiating $\langle X,X\rangle=H^{-2}$ twice gives $\langle X,X''\rangle=-\langle X',X'\rangle=0$; because $\langle X,X\rangle=H^{-2}>0$, $f=0$. Therefore $X(\lambda)=X_0+(\lambda-\lambda_0)V$ with constant null $V$ and $\langle X_0,V\rangle=0$. This entire affine line remains on the hyperboloid, so every null geodesic extends through every finite affine parameter; in particular all future null geodesics are complete.

Fix $\tau_0<0$ and set $S_{\tau_0}=\{\tau=\tau_0,\chi=\pi/2\}$. This is a smooth embedded equatorial $S^2$ with positive induced metric $q_S=a(\tau_0)^2\gamma_{S^2}$ and is compact by [F1], [F8]. Its future null normals $\ell=\partial_\tau+a^{-1}\partial_\chi$ and $k=\partial_\tau-a^{-1}\partial_\chi$ satisfy $g(\ell,\ell)=g(k,k)=0$, $g(\ell,k)=-2$, and $g(\ell,N)=g(k,N)=-1$, so they are normalized future null normals by [F7].
By [F6] and [F9], the assumed Axiom of Choice supplies Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, so the existence of $\Sigma_0$ makes $M_H$ globally hyperbolic.

Since $a''=H^2a$ and $1+a'^2=H^2a^2$, [F2] and step 1.3 give $\operatorname{Ric}_{\tau\tau}=-3H^2$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{\chi\chi}=3H^2a^2$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{\tau\chi}=0$, and $\operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=3H^2r^2\gamma_{ij}$. Thus $\operatorname{Ric}=3H^2g$ on the regular spherical chart; both tensors are smooth on the global hyperboloid, so equality extends by continuity to the two poles. Consequently $\operatorname{Ric}(v,v)=3H^2g(v,v)=0$ for every null vector.

The mixed Christoffel symbols in [F2] give $\nabla_X\partial_\tau=(a'/a)X$ and $\nabla_X\partial_\chi=(\partial_\chi r/r)X=(\cot\chi)X$ for every angular tangent vector $X$. Thus at $\chi=\pi/2$, $\chi_\ell=(a'/a)q_S$ and $\chi_k=(a'/a)q_S$. Tracing in two dimensions gives $\theta_\ell=\theta_k=2a'/a=2H\tanh(H\tau_0)<0$. So $S_{\tau_0}$ is future trapped by [F3].

The spacetime is globally hyperbolic by step 2.1, has the compact trapped surface of step 2.3, satisfies the null Ricci condition by step 2.2, and is future null complete by step 1.4. By [F9] and the assumed AC, the choice hypotheses of [F10] also hold, so [F10] gives compactness of $E^+(S_{\tau_0})$, consistently with the compact Cauchy slices in step 1.2.

By [F13], applied to the complete timelike product flow $\Psi$ from step 1.1 and the compact slice $\Sigma_0$ from step 1.2, every smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface of $M_H$ is diffeomorphic to $\Sigma_0$ and hence compact. The model satisfies AC, global hyperbolicity, the compact trapped-surface, and null-Ricci hypotheses of [F11], but has no connected noncompact smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface. It is therefore outside the theorem’s scope while remaining future null complete; the noncompact-Cauchy condition cannot simply be omitted.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and its induced Euclidean metric $d_2$ ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms). For $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $r>0$, put

$$\overline B_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2\le r\},\qquad S_2(c,r):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lVert x-c\rVert_2=r\}.$$

These are respectively the **Euclidean closed ball** and **Euclidean sphere** with centre $c$ and radius $r$. They carry the subspace topology inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Subspace topology: the traces of the open sets, its closed sets and its bases, the continuity of the inclusion, and the characteristic property of a map into a subspace). Since $d_2(c,x)=\lVert x-c\rVert_2$, they are precisely the closed ball and sphere $\bar B(c,r)$ and $S(c,r)$ of the metric-space definition (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space).

For the unit sphere centred at the origin write

$$S^{n-1}:=S_2(0,1).$$

The exponent is notation for this particular sphere, not a claim that a dimension theory has been developed here.

Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a nonempty open set with global coordinates
$y=(y^0,y^1)$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]),
let $(q_{AB})$ be a smooth symmetric $2\times2$ matrix of functions on $V$
with

$$\Delta_q(y):=\det\bigl(q_{AB}(y)\bigr)<0\qquad(y\in V),$$

so that $q$ is a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $V$ whose value
at every point is nondegenerate with inertia $(1,1,0)$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), and let $r:V\to(0,\infty)$ be
a smooth function. Indices $A,B,C,D$ run over $\{0,1\}$ and indices
$i,j,k,l$ over the sphere directions below. Define on $V$:

$$(q^{AB}):=(q_{AB})^{-1},\qquad \Gamma^A{}_{BC}:=\tfrac12\sum_Dq^{AD}\bigl(\partial_Bq_{DC}+\partial_Cq_{BD}-\partial_Dq_{BC}\bigr),$$

$$\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r:=\partial_A\partial_Br-\sum_C\Gamma^C{}_{AB}\,\partial_Cr, \qquad \Delta_qr:=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\operatorname{Hess}_{AB}r, \qquad z:=\sum_{A,B}q^{AB}\partial_Ar\,\partial_Br .$$

Further define

$$R^A{}_{BCD}:=\partial_C\Gamma^A{}_{DB}-\partial_D\Gamma^A{}_{CB} +\sum_E\bigl(\Gamma^A{}_{CE}\Gamma^E{}_{DB}-\Gamma^A{}_{DE}\Gamma^E{}_{CB}\bigr), \qquad R_{ABCD}:=\sum_Eq_{AE}R^E{}_{BCD},$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}:=\sum_{A,C}q^{AC}R_{ABCD},\qquad S_q:=\sum_{B,D}q^{BD}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}.$$

Let $S^2:=\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean
sphere with its induced smooth structure and round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]],
[[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]), let
$M:=V\times S^2$ carry the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]),
and let $\pi:M\to V$ and $\iota:M\to S^2$ be the projections. Define the
global symmetric covariant $2$-tensor

$$g:=\pi^*q+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$$

on $M$, where $r$ in this formula is pulled back from $V$. In any product
chart $(y^0,y^1,\xi^2,\xi^3)$, let $\gamma_{ij}$ be the round-metric
components of the angular chart. The components of $g$ are

$$g_{AB}:=q_{AB},\qquad g_{Ai}:=0,\qquad g_{ij}:=r^2\,\gamma_{ij} \qquad(A,B\in\{0,1\},\ i,j\in\{2,3\}),$$

Then:

**(a) The metric.** The global pullback formula defines a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ on $M$; at every point it is nondegenerate
with inertia $(3,1,0)$, so
$(M,g)$ is a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(b) Christoffel symbols.** Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection of
$g$, unique by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Let $S\subset M$ be a nonempty smooth embedded two-manifold, compact without boundary, whose induced metric $q$ is positive definite. At each point its normal plane $(T_pS)^\perp$ is a Lorentzian two-plane with two future null rays. On any open patch carrying a smooth ordered pair of future null normals $\ell,k$ with $g(\ell,k)=-2$, define
$$\chi_\ell(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\ell,Y),\qquad \theta_\ell=\operatorname{tr}_q\chi_\ell,\qquad \chi_k(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xk,Y),\qquad \theta_k=\operatorname{tr}_q\chi_k$$
for tangent vectors $X,Y$ to $S$. These are the null second fundamental forms and their expansions. A **future trapped surface** is such an $S$ for which, on every local patch and for both future null normal rays, the corresponding expansion is strictly negative at every point. Positive rescaling of a null normal multiplies its expansion by the same positive factor, so the sign condition is independent of its affine normalization and of a local interchange of the two rays.

When a specified conformal completion is supplied, write it as $(\overline M,\overline g,\overline N,\Omega,j,\mathscr I^+)$. Here $\overline M$ is a smooth four-dimensional manifold with boundary in the senses of [[def-topological-manifold-with-boundary]] and [[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]]. At each point $\overline g$ is a symmetric bilinear form on the tangent space, its components extend smoothly in every boundary chart, and its pointwise inertia is $(3,1,0)$ in the convention of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]. The vector field $\overline N$ likewise has components that extend smoothly in every boundary chart; it satisfies $\overline g(\overline N,\overline N)<0$ everywhere and $\overline g(\overline N,j_*N)<0$ on the interior. The map $j:M\to\overline M^\circ$ is a diffeomorphism onto the interior. The function $\Omega:\overline M\to\mathbb R$ is smooth in the boundary-chart sense, positive on $j(M)$, and zero with nonzero differential on the designated smooth three-dimensional boundary subset $\mathscr I^+\subseteq\partial\overline M$. On $j(M)$ the metric satisfies $\overline g|_{j(M)}=\Omega^2(j^{-1})^*g$, where pullback is as in [[def-pullback-of-a-covariant-tensor-field]]. The restriction of $\overline g$ to $T\mathscr I^+$ has a one-dimensional kernel at every point; this null line is the generator direction, and its future ray is the one whose vectors $v$ satisfy $\overline g(v,\overline N)<0$. Thus the designated boundary is null and future-oriented; no completeness of its generators is assumed.

A curve $\gamma:[0,1]\to\overline M$ is **locally absolutely continuous** when it is continuous and, around each parameter value, its coordinate functions in a boundary or interior chart are absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of that chart neighborhood, in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. Boundary charts take values in relatively open subsets of the closed half-space. To compare two charts around a parameter value, shrink its parameter neighborhood so the coordinate image lies in a compact convex subset of a local-extension domain of the transition map. Its derivative is bounded there, so the mean-value estimate ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]) makes the transition Lipschitz. Applying that bound to the finite disjoint-interval condition for absolute continuity shows that the transformed coordinate functions remain absolutely continuous; the argument in both directions proves chart independence. At an interior parameter value where the coordinate derivatives exist, $\dot\gamma(t)$ is the tangent vector with those components; the chain rule for the chart transitions ([[prop-chain-rule-for-smooth-half-space-maps]]) makes it independent of chart. A **future causal curve in $\overline M$** is a locally absolutely continuous curve for which, for almost every $t\in(0,1)$, this derivative exists and satisfies $\overline g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)\le0$ and $\overline g(\dot\gamma,\overline N)<0$. These inequalities make the derivative nonzero and select the future direction. On the interior, $\overline g(j_*v,j_*v)=\Omega^2g(v,v)$ for every tangent vector $v$, so causal character is unchanged, and the specified orientation condition makes the future cone agree with that of $N$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Define $\overline J^-_{\overline g,\overline N}(\mathscr I^+):=\{x\in\overline M:\text{there are }y\in\mathscr I^+\text{ and a future causal curve in }\overline M\text{ from }x\text{ to }y\}$. The **black region relative to this completion** and its **event horizon** are, respectively,
$$\mathcal B_{\mathscr I^+}:=\{p\in M:j(p)\notin\overline J^-_{\overline g,\overline N}(\mathscr I^+)\},\qquad \mathcal H_{\mathscr I^+}:=\partial_M\mathcal B_{\mathscr I^+}.$$ 
If no such completion is supplied, these two sets are undefined; their existence is not a consequence of the definition of a trapped surface.

Given in addition a designated smooth future null normal ray field $[\ell_{\mathrm{out}}]$ on $S$, called the **outward direction**, $S$ is **marginally outer trapped** relative to this choice when $\theta_{\ell_{\mathrm{out}}}=0$ everywhere. If the outward label comes from a side of an embedded spacelike hypersurface or from an asymptotic end, that side or end is part of the supplied data; it is not inferred from $S$ alone. The zero condition is invariant under positive rescaling of the chosen ray.

Assume Countable Choice for the smooth tangent-bundle and time-orientation conventions of the Lorentzian suppliers. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$. A **spacelike two-surface** is a nonempty smooth embedded two-manifold $S\subset M$ without boundary whose induced metric $q:=\iota^*g$ is positive definite, where $\iota:S\hookrightarrow M$ is the inclusion. It is **closed** when it is additionally compact. The constructions below apply to any such spacelike two-surface; compactness is not required. Its normal bundle is $\mathcal NS=(TS)^\perp$. Work on a nonempty open set $U\subseteq S$ carrying a smooth ordered pair of future null normal fields $\ell,k$ with $g(\ell,\ell)=g(k,k)=0$ and $g(\ell,k)=-2$; such pairs exist locally by the preceding lemma. No global pair is part of the definition unless one is explicitly supplied.

For tangent fields $X,Y$ on $U$, define the null second fundamental form, expansion and shear by
$$\chi_\ell(X,Y):=g(\nabla_X\ell,Y),\qquad \theta_\ell:=\operatorname{tr}_q\chi_\ell,\qquad \sigma_\ell:=\chi_\ell-\frac{\theta_\ell}{2}q.$$
Here $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection; its derivative of a section along $S$ means the pullback connection, equivalently the derivative of any smooth ambient extension along tangent directions. The preceding lemma establishes extension independence, symmetry of $\chi_\ell$, and positive definiteness of the screen metric. A **normal-frame boost** is the change $\ell\mapsto e^f\ell$, $k\mapsto e^{-f}k$ for a smooth real function $f$ on $U$. It leaves $q$ fixed; $\chi_\ell,\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$ scale by $e^f$.

A **null geodesic hypersurface congruence from $U$** along the chosen initial normal field $\ell$ is a smooth map $F:U\times J\to M$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval containing $0$, such that $F(p,0)=p$ and $\partial_\lambda F(p,0)=\ell_p$ for every $p\in U$, each curve $\gamma_p(\lambda):=F(p,\lambda)$ is future-directed and null, and its tangent $\ell:=\partial_\lambda F$ obeys the affine geodesic equation
$$D_\lambda\ell=0$$
along every curve $\gamma_p$; here $D_\lambda$ is the covariant derivative along a curve from [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. For each $p\in U$, let $J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$ be the connected component containing $0$ of the parameter values for which $d(F_\lambda)_p:T_pU\to T_{F(p,\lambda)}M$ is injective and the pullback form $(X,Y)\mapsto g(d(F_\lambda)_pX,d(F_\lambda)_pY)$ is positive definite on $T_pU$. Require, for every $\lambda\in J$, that its variation directions satisfy
$$g_{F(p,\lambda)}\bigl(\ell(p,\lambda),dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)\bigr)=0\qquad(X\in T_pU).$$
Thus its variation directions are orthogonal to $\ell$. For $\lambda\in J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$, the map $F$ has rank three locally near $(p,\lambda)$: its two section directions are spacelike and orthogonal to the nonzero null vector $\ell$. Its local image is a null hypersurface, with tangent space $\ell^\perp$ and induced radical $\mathbb R\ell$, as in [[lem-gr-fx-null-normal-plane-and-screen]]. The parameter $\lambda$ is affine. On each section in $J_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the **screen** is $\mathscr S=\ell^\perp/\mathbb R\ell$ with metric $\bar q([X],[Y])=g(X,Y)$; it is the positive two-dimensional quotient, identified isometrically with the tangent plane of that section by projection. The induced form on the full null hypersurface has radical $\mathbb R\ell$ and has no inverse. All traces and inverses in this definition are taken on the screen.

All screen bundles associated with this congruence are understood as bundles over the parameter domain $U\times J$: the notation $\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ denotes the branch determined by $(p,\lambda)$, so self-intersections do not identify distinct screen fibers. For each $\lambda\in J$, the screen Jacobi map $A_\lambda:T_pS\to\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ sends $X$ to the screen class of the variation field $J_X(\lambda):=dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)$; it is invertible for $\lambda\in J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$. A **focal instant** is a positive parameter in $J$ where $A_\lambda$ loses rank; the **first focal instant**, if it exists, is the least such parameter after $0$. Along an affine generator the screen derivative is $\mathcal D_\ell[X]:=[D_\ell X]$; it is independent of the representative, by the preceding lemma. On $J_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the derivative $A_\lambda'$ is taken using $\mathcal D_\ell$, and the **optical endomorphism** is $B_\lambda:=A_\lambda'A_\lambda^{-1}$. Its **optical expansion** is $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}B$, and its **optical shear** is $\sigma:=B-\frac12\theta\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr S}$. Since the congruence is normal to a null hypersurface, $B$ is self-adjoint. Its antisymmetric part $\omega:=(B-B^*)/2$, called the twist, therefore vanishes. At $\lambda=0$, $B$ is the endomorphism $q^{-1}\chi_\ell$ and these optical quantities agree with $\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$.

No orientation of $M$, $S$, or the screen is required for these constructions. Indeed, if two orthonormal screen frames are related by a real $2\times2$ matrix $O$ with $O^{\mathsf T}O=I_2$, then the endomorphism matrices obey $\widehat B=O^{-1}BO$ and $\widehat\sigma=O^{-1}\sigma O$. Cyclicity of the matrix trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\widehat B=\operatorname{tr}B$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\widehat\sigma^2)=\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^2)=|\sigma|_{\bar q}^2$; the last equality follows by summing the squared entries of the symmetric shear matrix in an orthonormal frame. This includes $\det O=-1$. The screen inner products and the rank of $A_\lambda$ are likewise invariant under changes of frame, so neither the index-form contractions nor the focal condition uses a signed screen area form. The preceding lemma constructs normal pairs using the supplied time orientation and only a local spacelike complement; changing the complement's sign interchanges the two future null rays. No global ordered pair follows. If an orientation is additionally supplied, the same formulas apply on that oriented subclass.

The preceding lemma establishes extension independence, symmetry of $\chi_\ell$, and positive definiteness of the screen metric. A **normal-frame boost** is the change $\ell\mapsto e^f\ell$, $k\mapsto e^{-f}k$ for a smooth real function $f$ on $U$. It leaves $q$ fixed; $\chi_\ell,\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$ scale by $e^f$.

A **null geodesic hypersurface congruence from $U$** is a smooth map $F:U\times J\to M$, for an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ containing $0$, such that $F(p,0)=p$, every curve $\lambda\mapsto F(p,\lambda)$ is future-directed, null and affinely parametrized, and each map $F_\lambda:=F(\cdot,\lambda)$ is a spacelike immersion before its first focal instant. The field $\ell:=\partial_\lambda F$ is normal to each section and tangent to the immersed null hypersurface swept out by the curves. The parameter $\lambda$ is an affine parameter. On each section, the **screen** is $\mathscr S=\ell^\perp/\mathbb R\ell$ with metric $\bar q([X],[Y])=g(X,Y)$; it is the positive two-dimensional quotient, identified with the tangent plane of that section. The induced form on the full null hypersurface has radical $\mathbb R\ell$ and has no inverse. All traces and inverses in this definition are taken on the screen.

Before the first **focal instant**, the screen Jacobi map $A_\lambda:T_pS\to\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ sends $X$ to the screen class of the variation field $J_X(\lambda):=dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)$ and is invertible. The first focal instant is the first positive $\lambda$ at which $A_\lambda$ loses rank. Along an affine generator the screen derivative is $\mathcal D_\ell[X]:=[D_\ell X]$; it is independent of the representative, by the preceding lemma. The derivative $A_\lambda'$ is taken using $\mathcal D_\ell$. The **optical endomorphism** is $B_\lambda:=A_\lambda'A_\lambda^{-1}$, the **optical expansion** is $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}B$, and the **optical shear** is $\sigma:=B-\frac12\theta\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr S}$. Since the congruence is normal to a null hypersurface, $B$ is self-adjoint; equivalently its twist vanishes. At $\lambda=0$, $B$ is the endomorphism $q^{-1}\chi_\ell$ and these optical quantities agree with $\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary with affine connection $\nabla$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior. A smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ is an **affinely parametrized geodesic** when
$$D_t\gamma'(t)=0\qquad(t\in I),$$
with one-sided interpretation at an included endpoint. Constant curves are geodesics. Unless another parametrization is explicitly stated, “geodesic” means affinely parametrized geodesic.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the
causal curves of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], and let
$S\subseteq M$.

**(a) Spacelike hypersurfaces.** A subset $\Sigma\subseteq M$ is a **spacelike
embedded hypersurface** when it is an embedded three-dimensional submanifold
of $M$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]) such that the
restriction of $g_p$ to $T_p\Sigma\times T_p\Sigma$ is positive definite for
every $p\in\Sigma$; equivalently, every nonzero vector tangent to $\Sigma$ is
spacelike ([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). A spacelike
embedded hypersurface is automatically a nondegenerate hypersurface, so its
$g$-orthogonal complement in $T_pM$ is one-dimensional and nondegenerate, and
it carries a unique future-directed unit timelike normal; that normal is
constructed where it is used, not here.

**(b) Achronality and acausality.** $S$ is **achronal** when no two distinct
points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\ll q$ or $q\ll p$; $S$ is **acausal** when no two
distinct points $p,q\in S$ satisfy $p\le q$ or $q\le p$. Every acausal set is
achronal, since $p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$.

**(c) Cauchy sets.** $S$ is a **Cauchy set** when for every inextendible
causal curve $\gamma:I\to M$ the parameter set
$$\gamma^{-1}[S]:=\{t\in I:\gamma(t)\in S\}$$
has exactly one element. Because a strictly increasing continuous surjection
of intervals induces a bijection of parameter sets, this condition is
invariant under reparametrization
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (e)); it is stated in terms of
parameters rather than of the point set $\gamma(I)\cap S$, so that a closed
causal curve counts two visits to the same point as two parameter values. A
**Cauchy hypersurface** is a Cauchy set that is also a spacelike embedded
hypersurface in the sense of clause (a).

**(d) Domains of dependence.** For any $S\subseteq M$ define

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and suppose there exists a Cauchy set
$S\subseteq M$ ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause
(c)): every inextendible causal curve meets $S$ in exactly one parameter
value. Then:

**(a)** there is no nonconstant future causal curve with equal endpoints
(so $(M,g,N)$ is causal and chronological in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-conditions-and-global-hyperbolicity]] clause (a));

**(b)** $(M,g,N)$ is strongly causal (clause (b) of that definition);

**(c)** for all $p,q\in M$ the causal diamond
$J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact; consequently $(M,g,N)$ is globally
hyperbolic in the sense of clause (c) of that definition.
